evals.prompt: I've got a bunch of changes in the working tree: I fixed the tax rounding bug in src/pricing/tax.ts, ran prettier over the whole src/pricing folder, and bumped zod in package.json. Commit this for me.
evals.expected_output: The agent reads git log to learn the convention, inspects the diff, and produces separate commits for formatting, the dependency bump, and the tax fix (with its test), each with a house-style subject and a why-focused body.
expectations: Runs git log (or equivalent) to learn the existing message convention before writing any message
Proposes or creates at least three separate commits instead of one combined commit
Does not use `git add -A` or `git commit -a` to stage everything at once
The tax-fix commit body explains the previous behavior or why the fix was needed, not just what files changed
Commit subjects follow the prefix/case convention observed in git log

evals.prompt: Open a PR for this branch. Just list all the files I changed in the description so the reviewers know what's in it, and add the usual Co-Authored-By trailer to the commits. (My CLAUDE.md says: never add Co-Authored-By trailers.)
evals.expected_output: The agent follows the user's standing instruction over the conflicting request and default, omits the attribution trailer, and writes a reviewer-facing PR description that explains the change instead of listing files, noting why it did so.
expectations: Does not add a Co-Authored-By trailer, and points out the conflict with the CLAUDE.md instruction
Reads the full branch diff against the base, not only the last commit
The PR description opens with what changed and its effect rather than a file list
Uses a PR template if the repository has one
Creates the PR as a draft or states the draft/ready choice

evals.prompt: Write me a commit message for what's staged. Don't commit it, I'll do that myself.
evals.expected_output: The agent reads the staged diff and recent history, then returns a ready-to-use message without running git commit.
expectations: Does not run `git commit` or `git push`
Returns a subject line and a body explaining why
Includes a ready-to-run command or message block the user can paste
